The Commission adjourned the hearing of the Petition after directing JIPL and BEST to file their written submissions, including the question of ‘arbitrability’ of the disputes. In compliance with the above directions, the Petitioner, JIPL, filed its note of arguments (dated 17.1.2025), including additional submissions vide an affidavit dated 27.2.2025, and the Respondent BEST filed its written submissions on 18.3.2025. 15. The Commission, after hearing the learned counsels for the parties on the question of arbitrability of the disputes, reserved its order on ‘maintainability’ of the petition, on 23.2.2025. Thereafter, vide order dated 12.6.2025, the Commission, after holding that the dispute is not referable to ‘arbitration’ and that the same is to be adjudicated by this Commission under section 79(1)(f) read with section 79(1)(b) of the Act., ‘admitted’ the petition, with directions to hear the parties on ‘merit’. The relevant portions of the said _26. BEST in the present petition has also raised issues on merit, stating that the claims of JITPL are barred by limitation and are also hit by the principles of constructive res judicata. Having held that the petition is maintainable, as above, we ‘admit’ the petition and direct the listing of the petition to hear the parties on merits, during the second week_ # **_ Issues involved in the present Petition are squarely covered by this Commission’s order dated 1.7.2025 in Petition No. 122/MP/2022 _** (iv) It is a settled law that a mere representation or correspondence does not extend the period of limitation [State of Tripura v. Arabinda Chakraborty, (2014) 6 SCC 460 - Paras 15 and 18]. Further, in terms of the Henderson Principle enshrining _Order II Rule 2 of the CPC and the principle of constructive res judicata_ , the Petitioner ought to have included its entire claim, including that of LPS, in the CIL Petition itself, as it relates to the same cause of action. The underlying question that needs an answer is whether the party could have/ought to have raised the issue before . In the the present case, the answer to this question is in the affirmative, i.e. the Petitioner could have raised the issue of LPS in the original Petition. (xii) The Petitioner has relied on the Commission’s order dated 1.7.2022 in Petition No.122/MP/2022. However, the same is wholly erroneous and divorced from the facts of the present case. In the said case, the Respondents did not contest the amount stated in the weekly principal invoices, nor did they deny that there had been a delay on their part in making payment. 19. After considering the submissions of the parties and perusal of the documents placed on record, the following issues arise for consideration: # **_ Issue No(B): Whether the claim of the Petitioner is barred by the principles of constructive res judicata as well as Order II Rule 2 of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908? _** 32. We have examined the above submissions. The grievance of the Petitioner emanates from the non-payment/delay in payment of the invoices by the Respondent BEST, pursuant to the Commission’s order dated 5.11.2018 in Petition No. 158/MP/2017. According to the Respondent BEST, the carrying cost and the LPS claimed by the Petitioner, in the present Petition, are not maintainable in view of provisions of Order II Rule 2 of the CPC 1908, and also in light of constructive res-judicata under Section 11 of the CPC, 1908. The Respondent has also submitted that since the Petitioner omitted to claim LPS in the main Petition and in the appeal, the Petitioner cannot be allowed to file a subsequent Petition to claim the relief so omitted. On the other hand, the Petitioner has submitted that the right to claim LPS arises only after the liability for LPS is crystallized, i.e., upon the payment of the principal amount, and since LPS is a continuous liability 37. In the present case, the claim of the Petitioner for LPS on the CIL compensation is premised on an entirely different and distinct cause of action than its claim for the CIL compensation. The former is premised on the Respondent BEST’s failure to make the payment of the invoices raised towards the CIL compensation and cannot be said to be a ground of attack/claim that is essentially connected with or incidental to the CIL determination involved in Petition No. 158/MP/2017 filed by the Petitioner. Similar objection was raised by the Respondent therein (UPPCL) in Petition No.122/MP/2022 filed by the Petitioner JIPL, seeking payment of LPS for the delayed payment of its invoices, and the Commission vide its order dated 1.7.2025, observed that the “right to sue” in relation to the LPS claims, begin to run only when there is a default in making the payment of LPS, which can only be subsequent to the crystallization of the LPS liability, i.e. date on which the payment towards the invoices has been made. The findings of the Commission on this issue are squarely applicable to the present case. We have, in this order (paras 24 to 29 above), while considering the question of limitation raised by the Respondent BEST, held that there is a ‘continuous breach’ of the provisions of the EOI/LOI for the non-payment of JIPL invoices by BEST and the ‘right to sue’ in relation to the LPS claims, crystallized from the date on which the payment towards the invoices was made by the Respondent BEST. Therefore, the contention of the Respondent that the present Petition is barred by constructive res judicata and Order II Rule 2 is not tenable. In view of the foregoing, we reject the contentions of the Respondent BEST and observe that the claims of the Petitioner towards the LPS are not barred by the principles of constructive res judicata as well as Order II Rule 2 of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, and the Petitioner is therefore entitled to the reliefs. Issue No. (B) is answered accordingly.
